newsitem.title: USA: Congress, nature obviate U.S. ag export subsidies.
newsitem.headline: Congress, nature obviate U.S. ag export subsidies.

text.p: Mother Nature and Congress will keep the United States from subsidizing grain sales for months to come, analysts said Friday, ruling out a revival of the transatlantic subsidy wars of the 1980s.
"It just doesn't look like we will need to use (subsidies) nor will the European Union or others be in the game either," said private consultant Bill Lesher.

In interviews with Reuters, Lesher and two other analysts said most factors weighed against cut-price U.S. sales. Speculation has waxed and waned for months that the United States would resort to export subsidies in late summer or early fall in order to dispose of this year's crop. The United States has not subsidized wheat sales since July 1995.

Chris Goldthwait, the Agiculture Department's sales manager, said Thursday there was no reason to employ export subsidies now, when prices were high and "we have sold what we have available to sell." In looking ahead, he said it appeared "prices and demand may remain relatively strong for wheat in coming months."

Analysts Mike Hoover of WEFA Group in suburban Philadelphia and Mark McMinimy of Washington Research Group said bad weather in Europe and North America set the stage for a possible tight supplies and reduced any impetus for grain export subsidies.

A mid-April freeze damaged the U.S. winter wheat crop in the southern plains and flooding has hit some northern regions that normally plant spring wheat. Both developments bolstered futures prices. In the next few days, the U.S. House of Representatives may vote on a bill to limit grain export subsidies to $10 million in the fiscal year ending September 30. Originally, $100 million was authorized.

Dry weather prompted the European Commission to announce Thursday it would tax wheat and flour exports, rather than discount its prices. One EU grain source said world prices might stay above EU prices through the summer.

The National Association of Wheat Growers has argued for months for a resumption in U.S. export subsidies. Lower exports will stunt prices and build up the U.S. stockpile, discouraging farmers from planting wheat. Over time, it could mean a "retreat from the world wheat market," NAWG said Thursday.
"Reactivation of the (Export Enhancement Program, the major U.S. export subsidy program) in time for the new marketing year could break this trend," NAWG said.
Agriculture Department forecasters will make their first estimate of the U.S. winter wheat crop in early May as wellas their first projections for the new wheat crop in competitor nations.

In recent weeks, U.S. attaches have filed reports suggesting a downturn in wheat production in Canada and the EU. EU output was pegged at 96.3 million metric tons, down 2.5 million tons, and Canada at 25.2 million tons, down 5.3 million tons.

Analysts have said freeze damage in the southern plains might reduce the U.S. winter wheat harvest by 100 million bushels. Last year, the crop totaled 1.49 billion bushels, two-thirds of the U.S. wheat total. Sowings of winter and spring wheat were down 8.5 percent this year. Freeze damage cut into hopes of high yields to offset the smaller sowings.
